lesson.title: Why Water Is Not Just Another Molecule
lesson.summary: This section explains why the bent shape and polar covalent bonds of the water molecule give it an uneven distribution of charge, and previews why this simple property has such far reaching consequences for life.
lesson.body:
Water, with the chemical formula H2O, looks unremarkable on paper: one oxygen atom covalently bonded to two hydrogen atoms. But two features of its structure, one geometric and one electrical, combine to make water behave in ways that turn out to be essential for life. The first feature is shape. The two covalent bonds between oxygen and hydrogen are not arranged in a straight line; instead, they meet at an angle of about one hundred four and a half degrees, giving the molecule a bent, or angular, shape rather than a linear one. This bend happens because oxygen's outer shell also holds two pairs of electrons that are not involved in bonding at all, called lone pairs, and these lone pairs repel the bonding pairs and push the two hydrogen atoms closer together than a straight line would allow.

The second feature is the polar covalent bond discussed earlier in this chapter. Oxygen is considerably more electronegative than hydrogen, meaning it pulls the shared electrons in each O-H bond much closer to itself. This leaves each hydrogen atom carrying a partial positive charge and the oxygen atom carrying a partial negative charge. If the molecule were shaped in a straight line, these charge imbalances might cancel out, but because the bent shape places both slightly positive hydrogen atoms on the same side of the molecule and the slightly negative oxygen on the other side, the charges do not cancel. Instead, the entire water molecule ends up with a distinct positive end and a distinct negative end. A molecule with this kind of separated, uneven charge distribution is called a polar molecule, and this single property, water's polarity, is the reason water behaves so differently from molecules made of similar sized atoms that happen to be nonpolar.

Because each water molecule has a positive end and a negative end, individual water molecules attract one another: the partially positive hydrogen atom on one water molecule is drawn to the partially negative oxygen atom on a neighboring water molecule. This is exactly the hydrogen bond described in the previous section, and it is the reason water molecules do not simply move independently past one another the way molecules in most other liquids do. At any given moment, a molecule of liquid water is hydrogen bonded to several neighboring water molecules, forming a shifting, temporary network that constantly breaks and reforms as molecules move, yet is never fully absent. This constant hydrogen bonding network is what gives liquid water its unusually high boiling point compared to similarly sized nonpolar molecules, since a comparatively large amount of energy is needed to break enough hydrogen bonds to let water molecules escape into the gas phase.

Water's polarity also explains why it is such an effective solvent for ionic compounds like the sodium chloride discussed earlier in this chapter: the positive and negative ends of water molecules can surround and stabilize individual sodium and chloride ions, pulling the ionic lattice apart and keeping the ions dissolved. This same polarity, and the hydrogen bonding it enables, is the direct cause of cohesion and adhesion, the properties of water covered in the next and final section of this chapter.
